Radiotherapy imposes dose-, fractionation- and radiation-type-dependent pressure, producing DNA damage, ROS, DDR activation and chromatin stress. Surviving cells may enter persister-like, CSC-like, senescence-like or hybrid EMT states. Local hypoxic, perivascular, CAF/ECM, metabolic and myeloid components can stabilize these states and support residual disease. Functional imaging and ctDNA provide selected clinical readouts, whereas spatial omics remains primarily a tissue-based discovery tool. Candidate combinations require validation against specific niche dependencies before clinical adaptation. Abbreviations: ALDH, aldehyde dehydrogenase; CAF, cancer-associated fibroblast; CD44, cluster of differentiation 44; CSC, cancer stem cell; ctDNA, circulating tumor DNA; DDR, DNA damage response; ECM, extracellular matrix; EMT, epithelial–mesenchymal transition; MDSC, myeloid-derived suppressor cell; MRD, minimal residual disease; ROS, reactive oxygen species; RT, radiotherapy; SA-β-gal, senescence-associated β-galactosidase; TAM, tumor-associated macrophage; TME, tumor microenvironment; Treg, regulatory T cell.

title: Intratumoral microbiota: spatiotemporal dynamics, microenvironmental immune reprogramming, and immunotherapeutic implications
abstract: The discovery of intratumoral microbiota has challenged the traditional view of tumors as sterile environments and revealed a previously unrecognized layer of complexity within the tumor microenvironment (TME). Accumulating evidence indicates that microorganisms residing in tumors are not merely passive inhabitants but dynamic ecological regulators that influence tumor evolution, immune remodeling, and therapeutic responses. However, the biological functions of intratumoral microbiota cannot be determined solely by microbial identity, but are shaped by microbial traits, spatial localization, tumor characteristics, and therapeutic pressure. In this review, we summarize recent advances in the origins, heterogeneity and dynamic evolution of intratumoral microbiota, while discussing emerging technologies and methodological challenges associated with characterizing low-biomass microbial ecosystems. We further highlight how intratumoral microorganisms influence tumor immunity and emerging microbiota-targeted strategies to reprogram the TME, with particular emphasis on microbiota-driven remodeling of adaptive and innate immune ecosystems. Furthermore, we discuss the emerging role of intratumoral microbiota on the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Importantly, microbial effects on immunotherapy are not only context-dependent but may appear paradoxical, with the same microorganism exhibiting opposing biological effects under different ecological and therapeutic conditions. By integrating microbial ecology with tumor immunology and therapeutic intervention, we propose a tripartite framework—microbiota–immunity–therapy—to re-evaluate the architecture of the tumor ecosystem and to position intratumoral microbiota as a dynamic regulator of immunotherapy response and promising therapeutic targets.

title: Targeting TEAD in cancers: paralog-specific biology, resistance and therapeutic opportunities
abstract: Abstract The TEA domain transcription factors TEAD1 to TEAD4 integrate Hippo signaling with transcriptional programs that govern tissue homeostasis and cancer progression. Their activity is shaped by cofactor engagement, palmitoylation, chromatin organization and extracellular cues, creating therapeutic vulnerabilities that vary with tumor lineage and cellular state. This review examines TEAD molecular architecture, physiological functions and paralog-specific biology, together with canonical regulation by NF2/Merlin and the Hippo kinase cascade and non-canonical inputs from mechanical cues, oncogenic signaling, metabolism and hypoxia. Particular attention is given to the distinct interactions of YAP1 and TAZ with TEAD and the contribution of alternative cofactors to transcriptional output. Across cancer types, the evidence distinguishes tumors with strong YAP1/TAZ-TEAD dependence, exemplified by NF2-deficient mesothelioma, from settings in which the pathway supports tumor plasticity, immune evasion and treatment resistance or may restrain tumor growth. These differences emphasize that TEAD expression or pathway activation alone does not establish functional dependence or reliably predict therapeutic response. Therapeutic approaches include TEAD lipid pocket inhibitors, disruptors of YAP1/TAZ-TEAD interactions, degraders, cofactor-switching compounds and YAP1-directed oligonucleotides. Early clinical findings with VT3989 in mesothelioma support the therapeutic potential of TEAD inhibition, while highlighting unresolved questions concerning patient selection, durability of benefit and renal tolerability. Priorities for clinical development include functional biomarkers of TEAD dependence, pharmacodynamic confirmation of target engagement and combinations guided by defined resistance mechanisms. Progress will depend on translating these mechanistic insights into durable antitumor efficacy at tolerable exposures in appropriately selected patients.

title: Oncogenic KRAS drives immune evasion through adenosine metabolic reprogramming mediated by NT5E and ADA
abstract: KRAS-mutant cancers are often resistant to immunotherapy and represent a major clinical challenge. The metabolic mechanisms by which oncogenic KRAS promotes immune evasion remain poorly defined. Using inducible KRAS cell models, human tumor specimens, and syngeneic mouse models, we combined metabolomic profiling, immune–tumor co-culture assays, and in vivo therapeutic studies to define how KRAS reshapes the tumor immune microenvironment. Adenosine metabolism was quantified by LC–MS/MS, immune infiltration was assessed by flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry, and therapeutic targeting was evaluated using genetic, enzymatic, and pharmacologic approaches. We identify adenosine accumulation as a key metabolic mechanism of KRAS-driven immune evasion. Oncogenic KRAS coordinately increases adenosine production through BRAF-dependent upregulation of ecto-5′-nucleotidase (NT5E) and suppresses adenosine clearance through AKT-mediated downregulation of adenosine deaminase (ADA). These complementary alterations result in pathological adenosine accumulation within the tumor microenvironment, thereby impairing T-cell function and promoting immune evasion. Genetic silencing of NT5E or enzymatic depletion of adenosine using ADA nanoparticles restored antitumor immunity and potentiated the efficacy of PD-1 blockade in vivo. Mechanistically, ADA converted the immunosuppressive metabolite adenosine into the immune-stimulatory metabolite inosine, thereby reprogramming the tumor immune milieu. In addition, pharmacologic inhibition of the adenosine receptor A2AR suppressed tumor growth in vivo by simultaneously enhancing immune activation and directly impairing KRAS-driven cancer cell viability. Our study uncovers a previously unrecognized KRAS-controlled adenosine metabolic axis that drives immune evasion. Targeting this pathway through ADA supplementation, NT5E inhibition, or A2AR blockade represents a rational strategy to overcome immunotherapy resistance with potential to improve the clinical outcomes in KRAS-driven cancers.

title: It takes two to tango: the intersection of deubiquitinases and m6A modification in cancer
abstract: The dynamic and reversible N 6 -methyladenosine (m 6 A) RNA modification has emerged as a pivotal layer of epitranscriptomic regulation in cancer, governing RNA metabolism and function. Concurrently, deubiquitylating enzymes (DUBs), key components of the post-translational modifications (PTMs) system, orchestrate protein stability and signaling pathways crucial for tumorigenesis. Recent evidence reveals extensive and intricate crosstalk between these two regulatory systems, forming a complex network that can influence cancer progression. This review systematically explores the bidirectional interplay between DUBs and m 6 A modification. On one hand, specific DUBs can deubiquitinate and stabilize core m 6 A “writers” (methyltransferases), “erasers” (demethylases), or “readers” (recognition proteins), thereby influencing RNA metabolism and downstream gene expression. On the other hand, m 6 A modification can regulate the expression of certain DUBs, either by influencing the stability and translation of their mRNAs or by controlling associated regulatory factors. This reciprocal regulation profoundly impacts key oncogenic processes, including cell proliferation, metastasis, metabolic reprogramming, and therapy resistance. By integrating current findings, this review highlights the significance of the DUB-m 6 A axis as a critical regulatory hub in cancer biology. Deciphering this crosstalk not only provides novel insights into tumor mechanisms but also unveils promising therapeutic targets for overcoming drug resistance and developing innovative anti-cancer strategies.

title: Mechanism-guided drug repurposing against therapeutically actionable resistance domains in cancer: from resistance biology to clinical translation
abstract: Tumor resistance remains a central obstacle in cancer treatment. It blunts the activity of otherwise effective agents and narrows the therapeutic window, so that patients may accrue toxicity without commensurate benefit, and it drives progression and relapse. Resistance is rarely a single lesion; it is the emergent product of interacting programs that limit intracellular drug accumulation through ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter-mediated efflux, provide extrinsic protection within tumor microenvironment (TME) niches, sustain the survival and plasticity of cancer stem cells (CSCs), and maintain quiescent dormant cells that seed late recurrence. Drug repurposing, the identification of new therapeutic uses for approved or clinically characterized drugs, is attractive in this setting because many agents developed outside oncology act on the transport, metabolic, stromal, inflammatory and stress-adaptive pathways on which these programs depend. In principle, existing human pharmacokinetic, formulation and safety data may shorten development timelines and reduce early attrition relative to de novo discovery, although mechanism confirmation and prospective clinical validation remain obligatory. Metabolic inhibitors, anti-inflammatory agents, antiparasitic and antiviral drugs have all been proposed to disrupt survival mechanisms engaged under therapeutic pressure, yet candidate selection and mechanistic attribution in resistant tumors remain difficult. In this review we apply a single mechanism-first filter to representative candidates in each of the four domains above, separating preclinical signals from clinically validated outcomes and stating explicitly where a conclusion rests on one primary study. We then examine how resistance biology can be linked to biomarker-defined patient selection. Finally, we consider the trial architectures, including basket, umbrella and platform designs, through which repurposed agents can be evaluated without diluting a context-restricted mechanistic signal.

title: Antibody-drug conjugates: mechanism, progress and future directions of cancer targeted therapy
abstract: Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) are a new type of precise therapeutic drugs that have been widely applied in the treatment of various solid tumors and hematological malignancies, especially for patients who have failed traditional treatment or developed drug resistance. ADCs are mainly composed of a targeting monoclonal antibody, a linker, and a highly effective cytotoxic drug. Through the antibody’s recognition of tumor-specific antigens, they achieve precise drug delivery and reduce systemic toxicity. However, ADCs clinical applications still face issues such as insufficient therapeutic efficacy and acquired drug resistance. Here, we summarize the structure of ADCs and focus on discussing the drug resistance situations of ADCs that have been approved by the FDA for various solid tumors. Additionally, we explore innovative strategies for the next generation of ADCs to improve the therapeutic effect of ADCs, providing insights for the development of new cancer treatment drugs using ADCs.

title: The PD-1/PD-L1 axis in cancer: from immune evasion mechanisms to next-generation therapeutics
abstract: Immune checkpoint blockade directed against the programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) receptor and its ligand PD-L1 has markedly transformed cancer therapy, producing sustained clinical benefit and prolonged survival in selected patient populations across multiple tumor types. However, clinical responses remain highly heterogeneous, largely limited by low overall response rates, the development of both intrinsic and acquired resistance, and immune-related toxicities that restrict the durability of single-agent treatment. In this article, we systematically examine the PD-1/PD-L1 axis from a mechanistic perspective, spanning its roles in tumor initiation, disease progression, metastatic spread, and immune escape. We detail how PD-1/PD-L1 axis drives T cell exhaustion, impairs antigen presentation, reshapes the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, and promotes epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), thereby enabling immune escape throughout tumor evolution. We further catalog recent innovations in PD-1/PD-L1-targeted therapeutics, spanning monoclonal antibodies, bispecific molecules, Fc-optimized biologics, and novel synthetic modalities—including RNA interference, CRISPR-based gene editing, antisense oligonucleotides, and mRNA platforms. In addition, we evaluate emerging small-molecule inhibitors designed to directly disrupt PD-1/PD-L1 engagement, modulate checkpoint expression transcriptionally or post-translationally, and reprogram oncogenic, metabolic, and epigenetic circuits to circumvent resistance. A dedicated focus is placed on deciphering adaptive and intrinsic resistance mechanisms, such as PD-L1 re-induction, T cell dysfunction, deficits in antigen presentation, and compensatory upregulation of alternative immune checkpoints (e.g., LAG-3, TIM-3, TIGIT). We also examine rationale-driven combination approaches that integrate checkpoint inhibitors with targeted agents, chemotherapy, metabolic modulators, and epigenetic drugs to amplify antitumor immunity. Taken together, this review proposes an integrated framework for understanding the diverse roles of the PD-1/PD-L1 axis in tumor–immune interactions and offers strategic guidance for the development of next-generation checkpoint inhibitors and precision immunotherapy approaches.

title: Tumor-associated CALD1 splicing variant driven by hnRNPA1 promotes colorectal cancer metastasis
abstract: Alternative splicing (AS) expands transcriptomic and proteomic diversity and is increasingly implicated in colorectal cancer (CRC) progression, yet the functional relevance of individual AS isoforms and the splicing regulators directing their generation remain poorly understood. RNA sequencing was conducted on five paired CRC tumor and adjacent normal tissue samples to profile the AS landscape and identify differentially spliced transcripts. Candidate isoform expression was verified by RT-PCR, quantitative RT-PCR, and immunoblotting. CALD1 isoform functions were assessed by gain-/loss-of-function assays in vitro and in vivo. To dissect the upstream splicing control and downstream protein interactions of CALD1S, we employed RNA immunoprecipitation, minigene splicing assays, RNA pull-down, co-immunoprecipitation, and mass spectrometry-based proteomics. Clinical relevance was evaluated using public datasets and independent CRC patient cohorts. Widespread AS aberrations were observed in CRC, with 1,048 significantly altered events identified. Among these, a short CALD1 isoform lacking exons 3b and 4 (hereafter termed CALD1S) was preferentially expressed in tumor tissues. Elevated CALD1S expression significantly correlated with advanced tumor stage, lymph node metastasis, and poorer patient survival. Functional assays demonstrated that CALD1S promoted CRC cell migration and invasion in vitro and enhanced liver metastatic dissemination in vivo, while exerting negligible impact on cell proliferation. Mechanistically, the splicing factor hnRNPA1 bound CALD1 pre-mRNA and promoted skipping of exons 3b and 4, thereby augmenting CALD1S biogenesis. Restoring CALD1S expression partially rescued the impaired migratory and invasive phenotypes induced by hnRNPA1 depletion. Furthermore, MYH9 was identified as a CALD1S-interacting protein and its knockdown attenuated CALD1S-driven cell migration. Clinically, CALD1 and MYH9 protein levels exhibited a strong positive correlation in lymph node-positive CRC tumors, and a higher combined CALD1/MYH9 expression was associated with unfavorable prognosis. Our study delineates an hnRNPA1-CALD1S-MYH9 regulatory axis that couples aberrant AS to CRC metastatic progression. These findings support CALD1S as a potential prognostic biomarker for disease progression in CRC.

title: Liquid-liquid phase separation in cancer radiotherapy and immunotherapy: emerging roles and translational opportunities
abstract: Abstract Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) is a physicochemical process through which biomolecules assemble into membraneless condensates via weak, multivalent interactions. LLPS has emerged as a central biological principle that helps explain intracellular spatiotemporal compartmentalization, signal transduction, and stress responses. Dysregulated LLPS contributes to tumor initiation, progression, immune evasion, and treatment resistance; however, its cell-type-specific functions and relevance to radiotherapy and immunotherapy remain incompletely integrated. In this review, we critically synthesize recent mechanistic and translational advances linking LLPS to cancer radiotherapy and immunotherapy. Condensates may either support therapeutic resistance and immune evasion or enhance radiosensitivity and antitumor immunity, depending on their molecular composition, subcellular localization, cell type, and treatment context. We examine how condensate regulation connects radiation-induced DNA damage repair with innate immune activation and evaluate emerging therapeutic strategies that target disease-associated condensates. We also assess LLPS-associated abnormal condensates as candidate biomarkers for prognosis and prediction of tumor response to radiotherapy and immunotherapy. Tissue-specific LLPS regulation across tumor types, dynamic condensate remodeling under therapeutic stress, and rational strategies combining phase-separation modulation with immune-checkpoint inhibitors and radiotherapy require further investigation. Integrating multi-omics data with artificial intelligence-based algorithms may help construct systematic LLPS-related therapeutic-event maps and predictive models, thereby prioritizing experimentally testable hypotheses for personalized cancer management. With rigorous mechanistic validation and prospective clinical evaluation, selective modulation of disease-associated condensates may enhance radiosensitivity and strengthen antitumor immunity.

title: circRAB6A-encoded KAPEP relieves PTPN6-mediated restraint on JAK-STAT signaling to drive KRAS-mutant colorectal cancer progression
abstract: Despite advances in targeted therapy, effective treatment of KRAS-mutant colorectal cancer (CRC) remains challenging. Although circular RNAs (circRNAs) have emerged as important regulators of tumorigenesis, the functional significance of circRNA-encoded micropeptides in KRAS-mutant CRC remains poorly understood. Integrative transcriptomic profiling was used to identify dysregulated circRNAs in KRAS-mutant CRC. The coding potential of circRAB6A was evaluated using bioinformatic prediction, internal ribosome entry site (IRES) reporter assays, and mass spectrometry. The functional effects of circRAB6A and its encoded micropeptide were assessed using in vitro assays and orthotopic and patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models. Mechanistic studies combined RNA sequencing, co-immunoprecipitation, bio-layer interferometry, and molecular dynamics simulations. We identify circRAB6A as a highly expressed circRNA in KRAS-mutant CRC, with elevated circRAB6A abundance associated with poor clinical outcomes. circRAB6A harbors a short open reading frame and encodes a previously uncharacterized micropeptide, designated KAPEP. KAPEP promotes CRC cell proliferation, migration, and invasion in vitro and accelerates tumor growth in vivo. Mechanistically, KAPEP directly binds PTPN6 and inhibits its phosphatase activity, thereby relieving PTPN6-mediated restraint on JAK-STAT signaling and sustaining pathway activation. Our findings identify KAPEP as a functional circRNA-encoded micropeptide that promotes KRAS-mutant CRC progression through the PTPN6/JAK-STAT axis. These results highlight the KAPEP/PTPN6 interaction as a potential therapeutic vulnerability in KRAS-mutant CRC.

title: CYP4A22-AS1 controls YBX1 nuclear accumulation to promote metabolic adaptation and radioresistance in cervical adenocarcinoma
abstract: Cervical adenocarcinoma exhibits intrinsic resistance to radiotherapy, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying this phenotype remain poorly understood. We integrated transcriptomic analyses of TCGA and an independent RNA-sequencing cohort to identify dysregulated long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) in cervical adenocarcinoma. Multiple functional studies, including clonogenic survival, proliferation, apoptosis, glycolytic flux, xenograft irradiation, patient-derived organoids, and clinical validation, were combined with RNA pull-down, RNA immunoprecipitation, chromatin immunoprecipitation, immunofluorescence, and rescue experiments to define the underlying molecular mechanism. CYP4A22-AS1 emerged as a consistently upregulated lncRNA in cervical adenocarcinoma and was associated with aggressive clinicopathological features and poor clinical outcome. Mechanistically, CYP4A22-AS1 directly interacted with the RNA- and DNA-binding protein YBX1, promoted its nuclear accumulation, and enhanced YBX1 recruitment to the glycolytic enzyme PGK1 promoter, resulting in transcriptional activation of PGK1. Disruption of the CYP4A22-AS1–YBX1–PGK1 axis suppressed glycolytic activity, impaired DNA damage repair, increased radiation-induced apoptosis, and markedly enhanced radiosensitivity in vitro. Consistent with these findings, CYP4A22-AS1 promoted resistance to irradiation in xenograft and patient-derived organoid models. Clinically, elevated CYP4A22-AS1 and PGK1 expression correlated with unfavorable prognosis. Our findings identify a previously unrecognized lncRNA-dependent mechanism in which CYP4A22-AS1 promotes YBX1 nuclear accumulation and PGK1 transactivation, thereby coupling metabolic adaptation to DNA damage repair and intrinsic radioresistance in cervical adenocarcinoma. This pathway represents a potential therapeutic vulnerability for improving radiotherapy response.

title: Multi-target kinase inhibition overcomes KRASG12C inhibitor resistance and potentiates antitumor immunity via the ERK–RRM2 axis
abstract: Although covalent KRAS G12C inhibitors have transformed the treatment landscape for KRAS-mutant cancers, their clinical efficacy is limited by the prevalence of intrinsic and adaptive resistance. This study aims to identify novel therapeutic strategies to overcome this resistance and elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms. Sotorasib- and adagrasib-resistant cell models were established, with the latter utilized for high-throughput drug screening. Transcriptomic profiling was conducted to uncover the molecular mechanisms underlying the synergy between KRAS G12C inhibitors and cediranib. The therapeutic efficacy and immune-remodeling effects of the identified combination were validated using patient-derived xenografts (PDX) and immunocompetent syngeneic mouse models. Clinical relevance was assessed using TCGA datasets. High-throughput screening identified the multi-target tyrosine kinase inhibitor cediranib as a potent agent that restores sensitivity to KRAS G12C inhibition. Mechanistically, cediranib synergizes with KRAS G12C inhibitors to enforce durable ERK signaling blockade and prevent adaptive MAPK reactivation. This sustained suppression leads to profound downregulation of ribonucleotide reductase subunit M2 (RRM2), a rate-limiting enzyme in deoxyribonucleoside triphosphate (dNTP) biosynthesis. Consequently, nucleotide depletion triggers catastrophic replication stress and DNA damage. Analysis of TCGA datasets confirmed that high RRM2 expression correlates with poor prognosis in KRAS-mutant lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PAAD) cohorts. Crucially, the resulting genomic instability triggers the cGAS–STING pathway, reprogramming the tumor microenvironment by enhancing the infiltration and activation of cytotoxic CD8 + T cells. In vivo, the combination achieved robust tumor regression with a favorable safety profile. Our findings define a druggable ERK–RRM2 axis that links metabolic vulnerabilities to antitumor immunity. This study highlights the combination of cediranib and KRAS G12C inhibitors as a promising translational strategy to overcome resistance in KRAS-mutant cancers.

title: FDX1-independent non-canonical cuproptosis establishes a parallel mitochondria-centric death program
abstract: Abstract Objectives Copper is an essential redox cofactor required for mitochondrial respiration and antioxidant defense, yet its dysregulation creates a therapeutic vulnerability that can be exploited by copper active agents. Elesclomol and neocuproine are two potent copper active compounds, but whether they induce the same form of cuproptosis , a copper-dependent cell death mechanism, has remained unclear. We aimed to elucidate the cytotoxic programs triggered by these two agents and to determine whether distinct mechanistic forms of cuproptosis exist. Methods Our study integrates limited-proteolysis proteomics to identify compound-responsive changes in protein structural accessibility, whole-genome CRISPRa (activation) screening, transcriptomic analysis of 436 CCLE cancer cell lines, mass spectrometry-based analysis of cellular and tumor copper abundance, genetic perturbation studies, mitochondrial functional assays, and mitophagy analyses. Pathway enrichment and functional validation were used to identify adaptive survival programs and compound-specific copper-handling mechanisms. Results Building on the previously established FDX1-dependent cuproptosis mechanism induced by elesclomol, we designate this pathway as canonical cuproptosis (c-CPX) and identify neocuproine as inducing a mechanistically distinct, FDX1-independent form of cuproptosis, which we term non-canonical cuproptosis (nc-CPX). In c-CPX, FDX1 mediates elesclomol delivered Cu(II) to Cu(I) reduction, leading to rapid oligomerization of lipoylated mitochondrial proteins and subsequent proteotoxic stress. In contrast, neocuproine induces n-CPX, a FDX1-independent copper-dependent death program that preferentially engages neocuproine stabilized Cu(I)-handling and stress-adaptation networks. Despite its FDX1 independence, neocuproine rapidly induces oligomerization of lipoylated DLAT, identifying an early point of convergence with canonical cuproptosis. Large-scale analysis of CCLE cancer cell lines further revealed that sensitivity to both neocuproine and elesclomol is associated with enrichment of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) transcriptional programs. Notably, neocuproine-sensitive cancer cells additionally displayed significantly higher mesenchymal/EMT scores across multiple independent gene-expression signatures, linking an OXPHOS-enriched, mesenchymal cell state to increased susceptibility to neocuproine-induced copper-dependent cell death. Limited-proteolysis profiling identified ATOX1 among the prominent neocuproine-responsive proteins. Functional validation demonstrated that ATOX1 depletion partially attenuates neocuproine-induced cytotoxicity, but not elesclomol toxicity, while ATOX1 loss itself promotes DLAT oligomerization, supporting a specific contribution of ATOX1-dependent Cu(I) handling to nc-CPX. CRISPRa screening further revealed that adaptive programs enriched during neocuproine exposure predominantly involve proteasomal and lysosomal pathways; whereas elesclomol is associated with distinct signaling and bioenergetic programs, including PI3K, JAK–STAT, and MAPK pathways, as well as oxidative phosphorylation and glutathione metabolism. The functional relevance of the neocuproine-associated pathways was supported by enhanced cytotoxicity upon pharmacological inhibition of proteasomal or lysosomal function. Despite their divergent initiation mechanisms, both canonical and non-canonical cuproptosis converge on early oligomerization of lipoylated mitochondrial proteins followed by Fe–S-protein loss, respiratory-chain dysfunction, mitochondrial remodeling, impaired mitochondrial quality control, and respiratory failure. Both compounds also induce cytoplasmic and mitochondrial ROS and late apoptotic features. Continuous N-acetylcysteine (NAC) exposure reduced the labile intracellular Cu(I) signal and rescued cytotoxicity; whereas NAC pretreatment followed by washout did not protect against subsequent neocuproine or elesclomol exposure. Together with the lack of rescue by caspase inhibition and the delayed appearance of apoptotic features, these findings support ROS accumulation and apoptosis as predominantly downstream consequences rather than defining initiating mechanisms. Conclusion Our findings establish a mechanistic framework distinguishing canonical FDX1 dependent cuproptosis from non-canonical FDX1 independent cuproptosis. Rather than representing separate downstream death programs, c-CPX and nc-CPX constitute distinct upstream copper-handling routes that converge on a shared mitochondria-centered proteotoxic program. These results provide insight into copper-driven cytotoxicity and suggest FDX1 dependency, ATOX1-dependent copper-handling, EMT/OXPHOS state, and proteostasis pathways as candidate biomarkers and therapeutic vulnerabilities for further investigation.

title: MAD genes from spindle checkpoints to targeted cancer therapies
abstract: Abstract Genomic integrity requires precise chromosome replication and segregation during the cell cycle. Disruptions in this process drive chromosomal instability (CIN), a key factor in tumor evolution and therapeutic resistance. Traditionally, MAD genes, including MAD1L1 and MAD2L1, were categorized as spindle assembly checkpoint components, whereas MAD2L2 was primarily recognized as a DNA repair protein. Increasingly, these genes are recognized as part of an integrated genome surveillance system, driven by shared structures, conformational dynamics, and interconnected regulatory mechanisms. Accordingly, the review redefines the MAD gene family as a coordinated axis for genomic stability, governed by conserved HORMA domains. The unique structural features, conformational plasticity, and protein–protein interaction interfaces of MAD-family proteins present unexplored therapeutic opportunities. Understanding these properties and their interaction networks may reveal cancer-specific vulnerabilities and facilitate the development of selective therapeutic strategies, including approaches to overcome therapeutic resistance, particularly in cancers characterized by high chromosomal instability.

title: Increasing cancer stemness drives prostate cancer progression, plasticity, therapy resistance and poor patient survival
abstract: Abstract Background Cancer progression is often accompanied by dedifferentiation and acquisition of stem cell-like properties (stemness). In prostate cancer (PCa), lineage plasticity and therapy resistance remain major clinical challenges, yet a unified quantitative transcriptomic framework connecting stemness, androgen receptor (AR) signaling, castration resistance, and disease progression across the PCa continuum is lacking. Methods We integrated 87,339 transcriptomic profiles from 33 preclinical and clinical datasets spanning the PCa continuum from normal prostate and treatment-naïve primary PCa (Pri-PCa) to PCa treated with neoadjuvant ADT (nADT) and metastatic castration-resistant PCa (mCRPC), with single-cell RNA-seq analyses encompassing 115,197 cells. Cancer stemness was quantified using a transcriptome-derived mRNA-based Stemness Index (mRNAsi; hereafter Stemness), and a 12-gene PCa-Stem signature was developed to capture PCa-specific stemness. Stemness, PCa-Stem, canonical AR activity (c_AR-A), castration-reprogrammed AR activity (cr_AR-A), RB1 -loss, PTEN -loss, and MYC activity signatures were quantified across cohorts. Functional validation included MYC inhibition and representative PCa-Stem signature gene depletion in PCa models. Clinical prognostic significance was evaluated in independent patient cohorts. Results The Stemness score and c_AR-A increased concordantly during early prostate tumorigenesis but diverged with PCa progression: as Gleason grade increased, c_AR-A declined while Stemness continually increased. mCRPC exhibited the highest Stemness and lowest c_AR-A, a pattern recapitulated in Pten / Rb1 / Trp53 -deficient mouse models. Global Stemness increased progressively across the PCa continuum, was enriched in aggressive PAM50-LumB and PCS1 subtypes, associated with proliferative and lineage plasticity programs, and predicted poor patient survival. The newly derived 12-gene PCa-Stem signature provided a PCa-specific molecular representation of Stemness and tracked disease progression and poor patient survival. Network analyses identified a coordinated mitotic regulatory program linking MYC activity, RB1 -loss, cr_AR-A, and the PCa-Stem signature. Spatial and single-cell transcriptomic analyses localized the PCa-Stem program to lineage plasticity-related epithelial cells and demonstrated progressive expansion of PCa-Stem⁺ epithelial cells during PCa progression. Functional perturbation of representative PCa-Stem signature genes, as well as genetic and pharmacological MYC inhibition, consistently suppressed Stemness-associated phenotypes in diverse PCa models. Conclusions Cancer Stemness quantitatively captures PCa aggressiveness, lineage plasticity, treatment resistance, disease progression, and poor patient survival. cr_AR-A, RB1 loss, and MYC activation cooperate to reinforce the high-Stemness state and therapy resistance in mCRPC. Collectively, our work establishes a trajectory-integrated transcriptomic framework defining cancer Stemness as a quantifiable molecular and clinical determinant of PCa aggressiveness, lineage plasticity, disease progression, therapy resistance and patient survival.

title: Bidirectional crosstalk between RNA modification networks and metabolic reprogramming in hepatocellular carcinoma
abstract: Metabolic reprogramming is a defining feature of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), enabling malignant cells to sustain proliferation, adapt to nutrient and oxygen limitation, evade antitumor immunity, and survive therapeutic stress. Emerging evidence indicates that RNA modification networks provide an important interface between metabolic states and post-transcriptional gene regulation. RNA modifications and their associated writers, erasers, and readers can reshape glucose, lipid, and amino acid metabolism by regulating RNA stability, translation, processing, and RNA–protein interactions. Conversely, nutrient availability, glycolytic activity, and metabolites such as lactate, acetyl-CoA, and S-adenosylmethionine can influence RNA-modifying enzymes, modification abundance, reader activity, and RNA fate, thereby establishing reciprocal metabolic–RNA regulatory circuits. Importantly, however, the functions of RNA-modification-associated proteins are not invariably modification-dependent; several regulators also exert catalytic-independent or non-canonical effects through protein interactions, chromatin regulation, or metabolic signaling. Distinguishing these mechanisms is therefore essential for defining genuine epitranscriptomic regulation. These reciprocal networks extend beyond tumor-cell-autonomous metabolism to influence redox homeostasis, ferroptosis and cuproptosis, cancer stemness, tumor immunity, and therapeutic resistance. Long non-coding RNAs and circular RNAs further intersect with RNA modification machinery as regulators, scaffolds, and, in some contexts, modification substrates, adding another layer of metabolic plasticity. Here, we critically discuss how major RNA modifications, with particular emphasis on m⁶A and the emerging but less extensively characterized roles of m⁵C, m⁷G, ac⁴C, and other modifications, interface with glucose, lipid, and amino acid metabolism in HCC. We further examine how metabolic remodeling feeds back on RNA-modification machinery and modification-dependent RNA regulation, while distinguishing these effects from modification-independent functions of the same regulators. Non-coding RNA crosstalk, tumor immunometabolism, regulated cell death, and therapeutic adaptation are also integrated into this framework. Finally, we evaluate therapeutic strategies targeting RNA-modification machinery or downstream metabolic dependencies in combination with targeted therapy, chemotherapy, ferroptosis or cuproptosis induction, and immune checkpoint blockade. We highlight persistent challenges, including uneven mechanistic evidence across RNA modification classes, limited site-specific causal validation, insufficient metabolic-flux measurements, catalytic-independent functions of modification-associated proteins, and unresolved cell-type and spatial heterogeneity. A more rigorous distinction between RNA modification-dependent and modification-independent mechanisms will be critical for identifying context-specific vulnerabilities and translating metabolic–RNA regulatory networks into biomarker-guided precision therapy for HCC.

title: Polystyrene nanoplastics promote colorectal tumorigenesis via gut microbiota-metabolite-Th17 cell axis
abstract: Nanoplastics (NPs) have emerged as pervasive environmental contaminants, yet their role in colorectal cancer (CRC) pathogenesis remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that chronic oral exposure to polystyrene nanoplastics (PS-NPs) promotes colorectal tumorigenesis in a murine azoxymethane/dextran sulfate sodium (AOM/DSS)-induced CRC model through disruption of the gut microbiota–metabolite–immune axis. Mechanistically, PS-NPs accumulate predominantly in the colon and cause structural damage to intestinal epithelial microvilli. PS-NPs induce gut microbiota dysbiosis characterized by depletion of the beneficial bacterium Faecalibaculum rodentium ( F. rodentium ) and a consequent reduction in its protective metabolite, propionic acid. This metabolic perturbation attenuates Th17 cell differentiation and IL-17 A production, thereby impairing anti-tumor immunity. Clinically, we detected diverse microplastics in CRC patient tissues and blood. Collectively, our multi-omics and functional analyses delineate a mechanistic pathway linking environmental NPs exposure to colorectal carcinogenesis via the F. rodentium –propionic acid–Th17 cell axis, highlighting the gut microbiome and its metabolites as potential targets for intervention against pollution-associated cancer risks.

title: Pyroptosis-metabolism crosstalk: rewiring tumor pathogenesis for precision therapeutic breakthroughs
abstract: Pyroptosis is a gasdermin (GSDM)-mediated lytic form of regulated cell death (RCD) that can either enhance antitumor immunity or maintain tumor-promoting inflammation, depending on the cellular source, signaling intensity, timing, and composition of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME). Metabolic reprogramming, a hallmark of cancer, can regulate pyroptosis at multiple levels, including inflammasome priming, cysteine-aspartic protease (caspase) activation, GSDM expression and cleavage, membrane pore formation, and cytokine release. Conversely, pyroptosis may influence tumor metabolism through the release of interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), interleukin-18 (IL-18), damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), and extracellular vesicles (EVs), and may thereby alter nutrient utilization, oxygen availability, immune-cell recruitment, and inflammatory feedback loops; however, direct tumor-specific causal evidence for this reverse direction remains limited. This review advances beyond a pathway catalog by applying a four-level evidence hierarchy: Level I direct cancer-specific causality, Level II tumor-context cell-resolved mechanisms, Level III mechanistic evidence from non-cancer models, and Level IV correlative or computational associations. Further distinctions are made among cysteine-aspartic protease-1/gasdermin D (caspase-1/GSDMD), cysteine-aspartic protease-4/5/11/gasdermin D (caspase-4/5/11/GSDMD), cysteine-aspartic protease-3/gasdermin E (caspase-3/GSDME), cysteine-aspartic protease-8/gasdermin C/gasdermin D (caspase-8/GSDMC/GSDMD), and granzyme/gasdermin (Gzm/GSDM) axes, alongside an evaluation of the evidence supporting glucose, lipid, mitochondrial, epigenetic, and immunometabolic regulation. Finally, the review addresses potential reasons for the failure of pyroptosis-targeted metabolic therapies, identifies patient populations most likely to benefit or be harmed, and outlines how biomarker-guided trials should integrate GSDM activation, metabolic state, cytokine output, and TIME composition to translate this crosstalk into precision cancer therapy.

title: Correction: Novel humanized monoclonal antibodies against ROR1 for cancer therapy
Hippo pathway in cancer immunity: tumor microenvironment remodeling, immune evasion, and therapeutic targeting
abstract: Abstract The Hippo pathway is an evolutionarily conserved signaling network that controls organ size, tissue homeostasis, regeneration, and tumorigenesis. Dysregulated Hippo signaling, particularly aberrant activation of YAP1 and TAZ, not only promotes tumor cell proliferation, stemness, metastasis, and treatment resistance, but has also emerged as a central regulator of anti-tumor immunity, shaping immune evasion and immunotherapy response across the tumor microenvironment. In cancer cells, the YAP1/TAZ-TEADs axis promotes immune evasion by inducing immune checkpoint expression, suppressing antigen presentation, regulating cytokine and chemokine secretion, and recruiting immunosuppressive populations. In parallel, Hippo pathway components exert distinct effects on controlling the development, survival, differentiation, metabolism, and effector activity of different immune cells. More recently, dysregulated Hippo components in stromal cells, particularly cancer-associated fibroblasts and endothelial cells, has been implicated in immunotherapy resistance, adding a third layer of regulation to the tumor microenvironment. These cancer cell-intrinsic, immune cell-intrinsic and stromal mechanisms jointly influence key steps of the cancer-immunity cycle. Importantly, the immunological effects of Hippo pathway are highly context-dependent and vary according to tumor type, cellular compartment, mechanical cues, inflammatory signals, and therapeutic pressure. Therapeutically, emerging TEAD inhibitors, YAP1/TAZ-targeting approaches, and indirect Hippo modulators provide potential strategies to enhance cancer immunotherapy. However, whether their immune-mediated benefits are independent of direct tumor cell-intrinsic suppression remains to be clarified in future studies. In this review, we summarize how the Hippo pathway regulates tumor immunity across cancer cells, immune cells, and stromal cells, integrate these mechanisms into the cancer-immunity cycle, and discuss strategies for targeting Hippo pathway to improve immunotherapy response.
